b: Fear names the threat. Anxiety leaves you guessing.
Fear focuses attention. You recognize the threat and act. A car speeds toward you. You jump out of the way.
“I’m afraid the client will reject our proposal.”
Anxiety’s threat is existential. Rollo May said, “…anxiety threatens the basis of selfhood.”
“I don’t know where I fit anymore.”
“I can’t seem to do anything right.”
“I’m overwhelmed, but I don’t know why.”
5 Questions to Turn Anxiety Into Fear
Help people move from ambiguous anxiety to specific fear.
Complaints about workload might conceal fear of failure. Resistance to change might reveal fear of becoming irrelevant.
#2. What’s the worst that could happen?
Ambiguous possibilities create helplessness. Naming empowers.
#3. What do you know for certain?
Anxiety feeds on imagined stories. Facts restore perspective.
Helplessness shrinks when people identify choices.
#5. What useful step can you take today?
Anxious people need more than solutions.
It’s dismissive to say, “There’s nothing to worry about.”
Say, “Let’s identify what you’re afraid might happen and decide what to do next.”
How can leaders help people identify a specific fear beneath anxiety?
